Prespecify the GRU initialization variants, checkpoint evaluation epochs, training budget and selection rule before viewing results. Recommended rule: maximize the four-category macro validation HR@10 over a fixed checkpoint grid; resolve equal scores by earliest epoch, and equal method scores by a declared priority. Keep seed 42, users, candidate identities/order and the host’s score-tie behavior unchanged; document ties without perturbing scores or modifying ranking. Treat the result as sampled-candidate HR@10: sampled metrics can reverse full-catalog rankings ([Krichene–Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)).

Compare methods through paired per-user hit indicators. Within category, report wins b, losses c and ΔHR=(b−c)/200; one changed hit equals 0.5 percentage points within category or 0.125 points in the four-category macro average. Recommended uncertainty: resample user pairs within each category, recomputing the macro difference for a prespecified 95% bootstrap interval. For category-level comparisons, exact McNemar tests use discordant pairs; matched-proportion intervals offer another option ([paired-proportion research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9447366/)). These quantify user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fixed candidates and trained models, not training-seed variability; ordinary intervals also omit adaptive-selection uncertainty.

Limit validation queries through a declared experiment list, checkpoint grid and stopping budget; log every attempted variant, including failures. Repeated checkpoint and method selection can overfit finite validation data ([Cawley–Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)). Prespecification limits discretion but does not remove winner’s bias. Label validation gains exploratory, freeze the final method before the host’s held-out evaluation, and restrict conclusions to the fixed-seed setting.
